stories.title: A guide to slash commands in the GitHub Copilot app
stories.summary: Slash commands are text shortcuts you type directly into the GitHub Copilot app's chat composer. By typing a forward slash, an autocomplete menu appears with context-appropriate commands for managing sessions, navigating projects, and customizing workflows. While some commands like /clear and /model work in both the CLI and the app, app-specific commands are tailored for the multi-session workflow the desktop app provides. File access commands such as /add-dir or /cwd aren't needed since the app manages project context automatically. The article highlights several commands: /plan helps break down tasks before coding and switches the session to Plan mode, /spar challenges assumptions and identifies risks, and /autopilot handles implementation steps. Additional commands include /rubber-duck for a second-opinion review using a different model, /create-canvas for building interactive visualizations, and /orchestrate for coordinating work across multiple repositories and sessions.
stories.snippet: Go beyond chat in the GitHub Copilot app with these slash commands. They'll help you plan, collaborate, automate, and customize your dev workflow. The post A guide to slash commands in the GitHub Copilot app appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

stories.title: How we took malware advisories beyond npm
stories.summary: GitHub expanded its malware advisory coverage beyond npm to eight major package ecosystems—PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, NuGet, Go, crates.io, and PHP Composer—by building an importer that ingests OpenSSF's malicious-packages repository, which holds over 15,000 OSV-formatted reports. The importer validates each record against the schema, rejecting and logging any that fail rather than quietly patching them, and skips entries originating from GitHub itself to avoid round-trip duplicates. Because the auto-published advisories now trigger Dependabot alerts without human review, the team added three safety layers: configurable batch caps that halt a run entirely if exceeded, provenance metadata tracing each advisory back to the exact upstream commit, and batch-level rollback that can revert a poisoned import as a single unit. Dependabot malware alerts are opt-in and begin matching dependencies against the database, including backfilled historical advisories, as soon as they are enabled.
stories.snippet: GitHub malware advisories no longer stop at npm. Here's how we wired OpenSSF's malicious-packages data into the Advisory Database, and why we built the pipeline paranoid. The post How we took malware advisories beyond npm appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

stories.title: How the GitHub legal team used Copilot CLI to streamline their workflows
stories.summary: GitHub's legal team, composed of lawyers, program managers, and business professionals rather than engineers, used GitHub Copilot CLI to build custom tools that streamlined their workflows. Principal Product Counsel Ngandu Kasuku created "terms-ai," a contract drafting tool featuring an internal drafting style guide based on plain language principles and a library of prior agreements. Since adopting it, she cut her review and drafting time roughly in half and achieved more consistent provisions across agreements. Online Safety Counsel Jesse Geraci began by analyzing source code for DMCA notices using plain-language instruction files, then expanded the project into a desktop app that handles contract review, NDA triage, risk assessment, compliance checks, and response drafting. Both emphasized that clearly defining methodology and standards enabled them to build serious AI tooling without traditional coding or engineering support.
stories.snippet: Learn how to build tools to simplify how you work—without writing a single line of code. The post How the GitHub legal team used Copilot CLI to streamline their workflows appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

stories.title: How to keep thinking
stories.summary: Working in tech in 2026 often feels frenetic, as engineers spin off tasks for AI agents and rapidly skim through their outputs rather than engaging in slow, careful thought. The author worries this habit is eroding their capacity for deep reflection and creativity. To counteract this, they recommend writing in your own words, since articulating ideas yourself forces genuine thinking rather than assembling fragments. Reading dense non-fiction books, and ideally writing about them, also helps restore slower mental habits. While AI-assisted work is now standard in software engineering, the author argues that losing the skill of careful thought would be a mistake, particularly for complex tasks like large refactors that demand taste and independent problem-solving.

stories.title: Giving and taking credit in big tech companies
stories.summary: Engineers in big tech companies must actively manage their visibility and take credit for their work, because managers cannot assess technical quality on their own and instead rely on quiet conversations with trusted engineers throughout the organization. Successful engineers write internal posts, mention their accomplishments in one-on-ones, and build relationships with their management chain. However, hoarding credit is counterproductive: sharing credit with peers gives them a reason to speak positively about your projects, since credit flows through informal networks that assess work at multiple organizational levels. Blame follows the same pattern, so projects concentrated in one person become easy targets when failures occur, as no one else is incentivized to defend them. Credit and blame ultimately translate directly into promotions, raises, and compensation.

stories.title: Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services
stories.summary: Enterprise operations depend on heterogeneous business systems that create data silos and process fragmentation, and traditional integration approaches like Enterprise Service Bus, API gateways, and Robotic Process Automation suffer from high architectural coupling, escalating maintenance costs, and limited intelligence. To address these limitations, the authors propose Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework that encapsulates existing enterprise applications as autonomous AI agents organized within a hierarchically nested structure. Layered stewardship topologies mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems, while each legacy application exposes a digital agent proxy that enables natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation. A central orchestrator coordinates these agents through task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, providing a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The paper introduces the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, and explores the methodology's generalization potential for heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data applications.

stories.title: The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models
stories.summary: The paper introduces the Ignition Index, a scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models by fitting a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting a steepness parameter β̂. Tested across 11 models spanning five architecture families, the metric demonstrates 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity through shuffled-label controls. The authors find that feedforward transformers exceed state-space models by 89% in aggregate β̂, with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. Additionally, Huginn-3.5B shows 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, while Pythia-410M displays a phase transition at training step 256 preceding induction-head formation. Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed. The work provides the first validated quantitative bridge between Global Workspace Theory's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability.

stories.title: Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models
stories.summary: Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks even when they possess the capability to solve them, frequently due to localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps. These bugs are often repairable by inserting a short patch generated by a weak probe model after the strong model's reasoning prefix, which redirects the trajectory toward a correct solution. However, this corrective effect is not reliably internalized through direct fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories. The authors therefore introduce Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. It contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

stories.title: From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction
stories.summary: A machine learning study investigates whether continuous predictors can be replaced by clinically informed categorical encodings for 90-day outcome prediction in acute ischaemic stroke without sacrificing performance. Motivated by a clinician user study calling for guideline-aligned cut-offs, the researchers compared standard and fully categorised gradient-boosted models on a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, with the categorised version using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. The fully categorised models were statistically indistinguishable from their continuous counterparts in two of the treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in predictive accuracy occurring in only one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remained consistent across all treatment groups, suggesting that discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors. The authors conclude that guideline-based categorisation is a viable design choice for stroke-outcome models.

stories.title: SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse
stories.summary: SKILLTRACE is a multi-trace provenance auditing framework designed to detect reuse of reusable skills in LLM-agent ecosystems, where skills are marketplace artifacts combining metadata, natural-language instructions, code, tools, references, and operational workflows. The framework addresses limitations of existing detectors, which target either single-modality source code or whole-package similarity and can miss reuse that preserves only one component. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces—Expression, Implementation, and Operational—with the Operational Trace represented as a Skill Operational Graph capturing activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only once during ingestion for operational extraction, after which audit-time comparisons run deterministically and each trace is calibrated against same-function strict negatives. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, comprising 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, the system achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further demonstrates that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

stories.title: Assembly Hall of Shame
stories.summary: The Assembly Hall of Shame is a GitHub repository that takes the opposite approach to typical instruction latency analysis, searching for the absolute floor of single-instruction performance rather than focusing on optimization. The project maintains a collection of test cases for numerous x86 instructions, organized into directories covering instructions like clflush, cpuid, fdiv, fsin, fxrstor64, fyl2x, idiv, mfence, mov, rdmsr, rdtsc, and many others. The current x86 champion is the fxrstor64 instruction, which appears to hold the record for slowest single-instruction performance. The repository includes supporting tools, a Makefile, and generates artifacts including an x86 leaderboard graph. By systematically benchmarking these instructions, the project highlights the performance worst-offenders in x86 architecture, providing a unique counterpoint to conventional optimization-focused latency benchmarks.

stories.title: Psychological Warfare in Reverse Engineering (2015)
stories.summary: REpsych is a proof-of-concept toolset that generates images through a program's control flow graph (CFG). Created by xoreaxeaxeax (domas) and presented at DEF CON, the project translates source images into functioning programs whose control flow graphs render the original image when viewed in a reverse engineering tool. The compiled binaries work reliably with IDA Pro and semi-reliably with other CFG viewers including Hopper, BinNavi, and radare2. To generate a program from a custom image, users save the image in the gfx/ folder as a 24 BPP bitmap and run "make image" in the project root, which produces two functioning binaries (repsych_v1 and repsych_v2) using different strategies for properly placing CFG nodes. The project has no specific practical purpose beyond demonstrating that the technique is possible, though potential (non-serious) applications are discussed in the accompanying DEF CON presentation.

stories.title: Captain Bible Reverse Engineering
stories.summary: The repository captain-bible-re by peterkelly hosts a reproducible environment and research notes for reverse-engineering the 1990s DOS game Captain Bible in the Dome of Darkness. The original game files are expected in a CB/ directory that is intentionally ignored by Git, while the FreeDOS/QEMU environment along with planned static and dynamic analysis are already complete. Two documentation outputs are published via GitHub Pages: a reverse-engineering documentation book under docs/ that records research progress, recovered formats, and executable analysis, and a clean-room engine specification book under spec/ that defines game mechanics and a portable compatibility contract for reimplementing the engine without relying on the DOS program's internals. Project planning is tracked in PLAN.md as a living checklist, with a full activity log maintained in docs/src/progress-log.md. The repository also includes a rust-engine directory and relies on QEMU (qemu-system-i386 and qemu-img) along with mtools utilities as runtime requirements.

stories.title: Show HN: Wyzer Programming Language
stories.summary: Wyzer is a statically typed, compiled, resource-oriented programming language that integrates distributed safety through choreographic programming and a Perceus memory model. The project is associated with Atiksh Sharma, who describes it with the quote "Simplicity is not the absence of power. It is power without pretense." The language was developed to address limitations that Rust leaves unaddressed, specifically distributed deadlocks, protocol mismatches, and cross-service correctness. By introducing choreographic programming, Wyzer aims to provide correctness guarantees across services and distributed systems. The repository includes documentation covering introduction, variables and types, control flow, functions and structs, and the memory model, along with a Discord community for contributor collaboration.

stories.title: Am I the problem? Interviewing another team to find out
stories.summary: The author, a DevOps engineer with a history of workplace conflicts—including a lost friendship after two years of arguments at Cisco—interviewed the infra team at ngrok expecting to find similar dysfunction. Instead, he found four team members (James, Stacks, Alex, and Sabrina) who navigated a major technical disagreement over adopting Argo Rollouts versus building custom Buildkite tooling with unusual civility, ultimately reaching consensus without animosity. Each interviewee accurately characterized the others' views, and none held grudges against those who disagreed. Comparing this healthy dynamic to his own team's frequent conflicts, the author realized he might be the common denominator across his past jobs. His reflections on this contrast, combined with years of self-improvement reading, prompted him to confront the possibility that he is the argumentative one.

stories.title: A shell exclamation mark is not for yelling. Be lazy
stories.summary: Shell event designators, available in bash, csh, tcsh, and zsh, let users reference and reuse parts of previous commands using the exclamation mark, following the pattern ![event][:word][:modifier]. Common examples include !! to rerun the previous command, !ssh to repeat the most recent command starting with "ssh", !$ to grab the last argument (useful with commands like sudo !!), and !# to reference the current line. Word designators like !:0, !:$, and !:* select specific arguments, while modifiers transform them: :h extracts the directory, :t the filename, :r strips the extension, and :s performs substitutions. For POSIX-compatible shells lacking this feature, the fc command offers similar functionality by letting users edit and rerun previous commands in their editor of choice. Users who find the feature disruptive can disable it with set +H in bash or setopt nobanghist in zsh.

stories.title: What are you doing this weekend?
stories.summary: People shared a wide variety of weekend plans, ranging from outdoor activities like camping in New Hampshire, group motorcycle rides through national parks, hiking, and street festivals, to relaxation activities including visiting family, playing dominoes, watching movies, attending concerts and BBQs, and celebrating birthdays. Many planned programming and tech projects, such as building a Python package repository to learn Elixir, working on Zig projects, refactoring a parser generator, migrating from FUSE2 to FUSE3, building a bare metal server, and developing a Social Maps API for OpenStreetMap with Google Takeout integration. Others planned to attend events like DEF CON, Long Island Retro Gaming Expo, or the Capitol Hill Block Party. Creative pursuits included working on a novel, reading "The Will of the Many," practicing photography, writing Wikipedia pages for bands, and playing Pokémon Platinum on a childhood DSi. Some respondents emphasized that doing nothing or simply going with the flow is also a valid and enjoyable option.
stories.snippet: Feel free to tell what you plan on doing this weekend and even ask for help or feedback. Please keep in mind it’s more than OK to do nothing at all too!
